Palatal approximant [j] followed by open [a] with high tone; the name means 'she tore'.

pronunciation.approximation: 'aw-YAH' — begin low in the chest on 'aw', then rise sharply to 'YAH'.

kin.label: Yoruba
kin.form: Ọya (also Òyá with tone marks), goddess of wind, storm, and transformation.

kin.label: Brazilian Candomblé
kin.form: Iansã, the whirlwind orixá of change and fire.

kin.label: Cuban Santería
kin.form: Oyá, syncretised with La Virgen de la Candelaria and Santa Teresa.

pronunciation.note: Ọya is Tier 1: the dot below marks a phonemic vowel distinction (open o versus close o) — a diacritic the ASCII form loses. Tonal variation, though crucial to Yoruba meaning, is not registrable in the DNS root zone.

domains.title: Lady of the Winds
domains.subtitle: Storms, Change, and the Cemetery Gate
domains.lead: Ọya is the orixá of wind, lightning, and radical change — the storm that tears down what is finished so that something new can grow. She is the only female warrior to ride into battle beside the thunder-god Ṣàngó, and she guards the threshold between the marketplace and the grave. Her name means 'she tore', and tearing is her ministry.

cards.name: Whirlwind
cards.desc: She arrives as a sudden gust that uproots trees and old assumptions.

cards.name: Warrior Queen
cards.desc: Wife of Ṣàngó and fearless general, she carries a sword and the irukere fly-whisk.

cards.name: Guardian of the Dead
cards.desc: She rules the cemetery gate and guides souls through transformation.

cards.name: Marketplace
cards.desc: Crossroads and markets are her terrain, where chance and commerce meet change.

symbols.name: Irukere (fly-whisk)
symbols.meaning: Her emblem of authority, whisked to summon and direct the winds and to sweep away what is stale.

symbols.name: Sword or machete
symbols.meaning: The blade that cuts away the obsolete and defends the community; swung by her possessed dancers at full speed.

symbols.name: Buffalo horns
symbols.meaning: Her kinship with the buffalo — the storm's brute force joined to maternal ferocity; in some rites the buffalo is her mount.

symbols.name: Nine colours
symbols.meaning: Her necklaces and cloth run to nine colours, especially burgundy and brown — the shades of the storm-lit earth and the graveyard's laterite.

mythology.lead: Ọya's stories are told in Ifá divination, Candomblé praise-songs, and the oral traditions of the Yoruba and their diaspora. She is change embodied, and her myths turn on thresholds — between sky and earth, market and grave, marriage and war.

myths.title: She Who Tore
myths.text: Her very name is her biography: Ọya derives from the verb yà, 'to tear, to split apart' (Abraham, Dictionary of Modern Yoruba, 1958). The name is a title of office. In ritual and story she tears whatever has outlived its time — she rips the old cloth of custom when it smothers the living, splits the storm front when the air has stood too still, and opens the ground between the marketplace of the living and the cemetery of the dead. To be mounted by Ọya in possession is to be unmade and remade: devotees whirl, brandish swords, and speak with the tearing voice of the wind. The mythology is exact about its own meaning: transformation is not a gentle persuasion but a rupture, and what refuses to be changed peaceably will be changed violently.

myths.title: The Secret of Lightning
myths.text: Ọya was wife and battlefield companion to Ṣàngó, and the traditions agree that she learned from him what no other orisha was taught — the secret of fire and lightning. Verger (Notes sur le Culte des Orisa et Vodun, 1981) records that when Ṣàngó's fortunes collapsed and he fled his kingdom, Ọya did not flee with him meekly: she tore at the sky with her winds, and some accounts say she cast herself into the river that bears her name, the Niger (Odò Ọya), rather than outlive his disgrace. Other lineages, especially in Cuba, make her the guardian of that disgrace's relics. The sources disagree about her end and do not care to reconcile; what matters is the pattern — she is the only one who shared the thunderer's power and the only one who did not abandon him. Her lightning is inherited, and inheritance is loyalty.

myths.title: The Buffalo at the River
myths.text: Candomblé narratives of Bahia tell how Ọya — Iansã — met the buffalo at the edge of her river and made an alliance with it: the beast's brute strength married to her whirlwind speed (Verger 1981; Mason, Four New World Yoruba Rituals). In the Ketu rites her dancers lower their heads and charge like buffalo herds; the horns that crown her shrines are the treaty made visible. The Yoruba sources behind the diaspora tale are sparser, and scholars treat the buffalo complex as a New World amplification of older river-storm imagery — but the meaning is continuous with the homeland tradition: Ọya governs the force that cannot be reasoned with, only ritually befriended. A community that honours the buffalo-woman is a community that has decided not to be trampled by what it refuses to acknowledge.

myths.title: Keeper of the Cemetery Gate
myths.text: In the diaspora liturgies and the older Ifá-related traditions alike, Ọya stands at the gate of the cemetery, not as death's mistress but as its border guard. Mason (1985) describes her ruling the passage between the market — the noisy, bargaining world of the living — and the quiet acreage of the dead; the hurricane that precedes her arrival is the escort of souls in transit. Devotees say she receives the dead the way she receives everything else: at speed, without sentimentality, and with absolute attention. The mythology resolves an apparent paradox — the goddess of life-giving storm as guardian of the grave — by refusing it: for Ọya, death is not the opposite of change but its final form, and the gate is simply the last threshold she is asked to tear open.

lore.syncretism: In the Afro-Atlantic religions Ọya became Iansã in Brazilian Candomblé, syncretised with Saint Barbara and Saint Teresa — saints of lightning, of decisive action, of the fortress under siege. In Cuban Santería she is Oyá, paired with the Virgen de la Candelaria; her nine-coloured cloth and buffalo horns identify her instantly in any botánica. In Haitian Vodou her winds blow through the Gede's cemetery humour, and in New Orleans Voodoo she survives as a spirit of storms and sudden reversals. Wherever Yoruba people were dispersed, Ọya travelled as the orixá of necessary upheaval — her whirlwinds, one might say, crossed the Atlantic itself and have not stopped turning since.
lore.culturalLegacy: Ọya remains one of the most honoured orixás in the African diaspora. She strides through the literature of the Black Atlantic — from Cuban letra del año pronouncements to Brazilian samba-enredo lyrics — as the patroness of the turnaround: the queen who loses the battle and wins the war. Her colours fly at every Candomblé ijexá; her swords flash in the hands of possessed dancers from Salvador to Havana. Feminist and womanist theologians have claimed her as a model of female force that is not domesticated by marriage, motherhood, or mourning. In an age of climate change and social upheaval, Ọya speaks with uncomfortable relevance: the storm is not cruelty — it is the only way the forest clears its own dead wood.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Ọya is the goddess we pray to when we are afraid of what must end. She does not promise gentle transformation. Her winds tear roofs from houses and uproot trees that have stood for decades. Yet without her, the air would stagnate and the soil would never clear for new seed.

To sit with Ọya is to ask what in your life has completed its season. She does not answer with comfort. She answers with a gust that slams the door and a flash of lightning that shows, for one instant, exactly what must go. Her gift is not the storm itself; it is the cleared ground that remains after it passes — and the knowledge that you survived the tearing.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is Yoruba: Ọya. Yoruba is a tonal language; the standard written form uses a dot below ọ to distinguish open [ɔ] from close [o]. The full tonal spelling is Òyá (low tone, then high tone), but tone marks are not registrable in the DNS root zone. The meaning 'she tore' derives from the verb yà. PUNICODEX therefore registers Ọya with the dot below, preserving the distinctive open vowel.

lore.archaeology: Ọya's material traces ride the storm: buffalo horns and iron swords from Candomblé shrines in Bahia, nine-strand bead necklaces in burgundy and brown, and the fly-whisks (irukere) whisked by her initiates, conserved in museum and terreiro collections on both sides of the Atlantic. In Yorubaland her presence is read in the Niger's storm seasons and in market-edge shrines where traders leave offerings against sudden loss — an archaeology of thresholds rather than temples.
